name: Muyu, Kawip/Kawiyet dialect
confidence_why: The only first-hand description of the Kawip/Kawiyet dialect, Zahrer's 2023 reference grammar, finds no lexical stress and Zahrer 2025 repeats this, while the word-level accent reported by Drabbe 1954 and Christensen 2013 concerns other Muyu varieties (Ninati and Yonggom) and is known only through Zahrer's summary.

catalog_quote: Evidence for lexical stress in Muyu varies. Both Drabbe (1954) and Christensen (2013) report the existence of non-phonemic accent/stress on the lexeme level for their respective dialect. According to Drabbe, an “accent” (which is not further specified) is on the last syllable of each word, and a “minor accent” (i.e. secondary stress) on the first syllable of a trisyllabic word. In contrast, Christensen reports the lexical stress ... always to be on the first syllable. ... However, our findings for the Kawip dialect point in another direction. It seems that speakers of Kawip do not assign lexical stress at all. Although we did not investigate the topic systematically, there are two kinds of (very preliminary) evidence for a lack of lexical stress. Firstly, when confronted with two contrastively stressed tokens of one and the same word, e.g. /"yu.lun/ vs. /yu."lun/, our consultants do not…

new_statements.quote: Unlike other languages of the Ok family, Muyu does not have lexical tone. Furthermore, there seems to be no lexical stress. Prosodic features take place in larger units, e.g. falling and rising intonation to signal finality or continuation in complex sentences (see Zahrer 2024).

new_statements.relation_note: Same coding as the catalog (catalog_kind no-word-stress, from Zahrer 2023 sect. 2.4.1) and already listed in the webcat record as 'confirms'; the only new detail is the locator correction p. 5 -> p. 6. Variety: the collection 'focuses exclusively on the Kawiyet dialect spoken in the two villages Upyetetko and Kanggewot in the central Muyu area' (sect. 1.1, printed p. 3), i.e. exactly the catalog's Kawip/Kawiyet dialect; the book also gives the glottocodes nort2916 (North Muyu) / sout2940 (South Muyu) in fn. 1, p. 4.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No lexical tone and (tentatively) no word-level stress; prosody operates at the phrase/sentence level as intonation (falling = finality, rising = continuation).
new_statements.exceptions: none; the statement is hedged ('there seems to be')
new_statements.identity_note: Zahrer 2025 describes exclusively the Kawiyet (Kawip) dialect of villages Upyetetko and Kanggewot (sect. 1.1, p. 3) and equates the language with glottocodes nort2916/sout2940 (fn. 1, p. 4) — the catalog's variety. Christensen 2013 is catalogued by SIL under Yongkom [yon]; Zahrer 2025 (p. 4) says 'Yonggom and Muyu seem to be two dialects of the same language (cf. Christensen 2013..)', but Glottolog and the catalog hold Yongkom as a separate entry (yong1280, coded fixed: initial syllable from Christensen 2002 OPD and Christensen 2010). Muyu has at least six dialects (Aree, Kawiyet, Okpari, Kakaip, Kamindip, Yonggom) that 'vary greatly in their lexicon and sometimes in phonetic detail' (Zahrer 2025, p. 3), so a stress statement for Yonggom should not be transferred to Kawip.

readall_conflicts: The one listed open work (Christensen 2013, Yongkom Reference Grammar) is not available online at either SIL archive record and was not opened, so nothing new was read from it. The only disagreement on record is the one the catalog's own deciding source already reports: Zahrer 2023 (sect. 2.4.1) summarises Drabbe 1954 as placing an 'accent' on the last syllable with a 'minor accent' on the first syllable of trisyllables (Ninati dialect) and Christensen 2013 as placing lexical stress always on the first syllable (Yonggom), against Zahrer's own preliminary finding that Kawip speakers 'do not assign lexical stress at all'. Zahrer 2025 (opened, p. 6) restates the Kawiyet finding as 'there seems to be no lexical stress', hedged; Zahrer 2024 (opened) is silent on word stress. So for the Kawip/Kawiyet dialect all opened material agrees with the catalog; the initial-stress and final-accent reports belong to other dialects/varieties and are not contradicted by anything opened here.

sources.quote: Intonation study only (contour clustering of 325 IU-final f0 contours: final verbs -> falling, medial/multi verbs -> rising/level boundary tones). On word prosody it says only that 'language-specific phonological categories (e.g. pitch accents) have not been established yet'; no claim about lexical stress.
sources.note: Silent on lexical stress; compatible with the catalog's no-word-stress coding (it describes prosody only at the intonation-phrase level) but does not itself decide it. Searched the full text for stress/accent/prominence: the only hit is the 'pitch accents.. not established yet' sentence above.
